rows.evidence: Q1: Methods and Results - own Landsat TM/ETM+ land-use classification 1995-2010 (overall accuracy 95.1%, Kappa 0.8977), own compilation of 59 groundwater-table wells and 74 quality wells 1998-2011, field surveys in 125 villages 2005-2013, Mann-Kendall trend tests (Table 5).
rows.notes: Remote sensing is used by the authors only as a monitoring tool for land-use/oasis area change; the study never reports that RS data were used by policy makers to set water quotas or reduce irrigated area. The reported groundwater-table rise of 45 cm (2005-2011, northern oasis, Discussion) comes from well observations and is attributed to the Ecological Construction policy measures (closure of 3,161 wells, water allocation plan requiring 22% of mountain runoff to reach Minqin, drip/tube irrigation, crop restructuring), not to remote sensing. The study therefore shows at most that RS can monitor land-use change (a precondition for RS-informed adaptive policy), not that RS delivered groundwater recovery. Groundwater table and runoff figures carry standard-error bars (Figs 5-6) and Mann-Kendall statistics, but these concern the policy-attributed trend, not an RS effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods and Results - own Landsat-based land-use mapping 1995-2010 (Tables 1-4, Figs 2-3) plus groundwater-well data and field surveys.
rows.notes: The study's own RS result is a change in land-use areas (e.g., shrub land increased from 116.71 km2 in 2005 to 160.10 km2 in 2010, Table 1), which the authors attribute to afforestation under the EC policy, not to remote sensing; this is vegetation-cover area, not biodiversity. The only biodiversity-type statement (vegetation types falling from 19 in the 1950s to 9 in 2010; replacement of meadow communities by halophytic/xerophytic shrubs) is cited from other work (Wang et al. 2002; Peng et al. 2004; Li et al. 2011) and shows degradation, not recovery. No own evidence that RS delivered any biodiversity benefit; RS is only the monitoring method.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods - own remote-sensing classification, runoff records 1962-2011 from the basin management bureau, groundwater-well data 1998-2011, and biyearly field surveys 2005-2013 in 125 villages.
rows.notes: Water-conservation outcomes reported in the Discussion (inflow to Minqin rising from 0.97x10^8 m3 in 2005 to 2.59x10^8 m3 in 2011; groundwater extraction down 2.4x10^8 m3; irrigation water efficiency 0.56 to 0.61; water consumption down 1500-1800 m3/ha; irrigation area reduced to 41,700 ha) are attributed by the authors to the EC policy package (well closure, watershed water allocation, drip and tube irrigation, crop restructuring) and partly drawn from the county Water Resource Bureau. The study does not report that remote-sensing data were used to set quotas or reduce irrigated area, nor any measured effect of RS on water use; RS is solely the authors' tool to map land-use change. The study also notes farmers' passive resistance to drip irrigation and well closure (Discussion), but this concerns the policy measures, not RS.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a policy-oriented case study of Minqin Oasis combining Landsat land-use mapping, groundwater and runoff records, and field surveys; remote sensing is the authors' monitoring method, not an intervention evaluated for its effects. The review's claim that policies 'used RS data to set water quotas' is not stated anywhere in the paper, so all three rows fail Q2 with the study supporting only the upstream monitoring capability.
